newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish pension fund equity investment seen rising.
newsitem.headline: Finnish pension fund equity investment seen rising.

text.p: Changes made to Finland's employment pension funds at the beginning of the year look set to free up substantial amounts of money which could boost trade and curb volatility on the Helsinki bourse.
The reforms aim to relax pension funds' stringent yield requirements, enabling them to increase their solvency capital and to venture into riskier sectors such as equities.
Employment pension funds receive contributions from employers and employees and are overseen by trade unions and the government.
The new rules governing pension funds allow them to boost capital without raising contributions.

Under the new system, the minimum required rate of return on investment falls to about 5.5 percent from six percent, while the rate at which funds are allocated to future pensions is temporarily cut to three percent.

The temporary 2.5 percentage point difference between the funding rate and the required return will be in force for two to three years, so that pension insurers' solvency capital can be boosted to work as a buffer for increased portfolio volatility.

Pirkko Alitalo, investment director at insurer Pohjola, said the system will let employment pension funds roughly double their investments in equities within five years from about seven percent of their portfolios now.
"The goal of the reform is to double employment pension companies' present solvency capital of about seven billion markka within the next couple of years," she said.
"This would improve the companies' risk-carrying capacity to the extent that they would be able to double their stock market investments in about five years," she added.
She said it was impossible to give a figure, but most of the new liquidity will probably flow to the Helsinki bourse.

"The clue to the whole reform is that pension contributions would decrease and they (employment pension funds) would get more profits from their investments," said Jukka Huuskonen at Arctos Securities.

Preliminary 1996 figures show that investments by the Finnish work pension funds -- which play an important role in statutory pension provisions -- totalled 205 billion markka, of which shares accounted for 7.4 percent or 15.1 billion markka.
Although investments in equities have clearly risen on 1995 -- when shares accounted for around six percent of total investments -- Finland is still well behind its Nordic counterparts.
Corresponding figures are around nine percent in Sweden and 16.3 percent in Denmark, according to the Finnish insurers association.
Shareholdings relative to the Helsinki bourse's market capitalisation -- 285 billion markka at end-December -- average about five percent.

The target is to double pension funds' equity investments, so about 10 billion markka could flow into stocks over five years, triggering a potential annual inflow of some two billion markka of new liquidity to the Helsinki stock exchange.
For Helsinki, where daily trading volumes averaged 405 million markka in 1996, that is a significant sum, analysts say.
"Two billion markka is a considerable amount of money, it would certainly bring a buffer (against volatility) and more stability," said Arctos' Huuskonen.
"The new flow of liquidity would also rationalise the pricing of shares," said Matti Ahokas, market analyst at Postipankki.
Although analysts expect the bulk of the extra funds to be targetted at equities rather than bonds, they saif it was unlikely that Helsinki-listed companies will be the sole beneficiaries.
"The problem is that big investors are already heavily invested in the large companies," Huuskonen said.
Investors could start seeking alternative investments among small and medium sized companies on the OTC- and Brokers' lists.
"The new liquidity would not be channelled only to the Helsinki bourse, small and medium sized companies would also get their share," Postipankki's Ahokas said.
Some of the money could be widely dispersed abroad, particularly if the single European currency becomes reality in the next millenium.
"A wide single market area would add new exchange-rate risk-free investment objects to the domestic offerings," said Pertti Pylkkonen, economist at the Bank of Finland.
"The risks associated with securities investments would be easier to spread more widely than is possible in the Finnish capital markets alone," he said.
But major flow of funds abroad are unlikely before the single European currency, as ongoing hedging against currency risks can get quite expensive, Pylkkonen added.
In addition, according to Finnish Social and Health Ministry regulations, pension funds need to grow their solvency capital before they can increase their currency positions.
